shots.phrase: Begin by framing Search Engine Architecture Overview as a question about inputs, decisions, and observable results.
Consider this worked case: A web crawler indexes HTML pages by extracting text, building an inverted index, and storing term frequencies.
This establishes the vocabulary and scope needed for the remaining sections.
Now define Query Processing and Parsing precisely enough that another learner could test the definition.
Consider this worked case: A natural language query like 'climate change effects' is tokenized and normalized to match indexed terms.
A precise definition makes later examples easier to evaluate and revise.
With the foundation in place, examine how Inverted Index Construction operates in a concrete sequence.
Consider this worked case: The term 'machine' points to document IDs [101, 105, 112], allowing direct access to containing pages.
The trace converts an abstract statement into an inspectable sequence.
Next, compare the choices involved in TF-IDF Relevance Scoring and make the decision criteria explicit.

Topics include search interfaces, traditional retrieval models (for example, TF-IDF, BM25), modern retrieval techniques (for example, neural reranking and retrieval), search engine evaluation, and search applications (for example, conversational IR, enterprise search).
Compare alternatives against the same constraints so the evaluation does not move the goalposts.
Apply BM25 Ranking Algorithm to a worked situation instead of treating it as an isolated definition.
Students may not take and receive credit for CSCI-536 and CSCI-636.
Work from the concrete inputs to the result, checking units, types, or invariants at each step.
Examine the tradeoffs in Neural Reranking Techniques, including what improves and what becomes more difficult.
Consider this worked case: A transformer-based model scores query-document pairs by analyzing semantic similarity in high-dimensional space.
Making the tradeoff visible prevents a local improvement from hiding a larger cost.
Stress-test the reasoning around Search Evaluation Metrics with an edge case and identify which assumption controls the outcome.
Query planning and physical storage affect performance without changing logical query meaning.
Change one assumption at a time and observe which part of the reasoning no longer holds.
Use Conversational and Enterprise Search to diagnose a failure by separating symptoms, causes, and corrective action.
Students will also review current IR research topics, and complete a group project in which they will design and execute experiments for search engine components.
Locate the first point where observed behavior diverges from expected behavior, then test the smallest plausible cause.
Connect Experimental Design in IR to the earlier ideas and explain how the pieces work as one system.
Supervised methods learn mappings from examples paired with target labels, while unsupervised methods identify structure without targets.
Explain each connection explicitly and verify that information retains the same meaning across representations.
Finish with Practical Analysis Checklist as a practical checklist that can guide a new analysis.
Evaluation must match the task and the cost of errors, while distribution shift, missing data, overfitting, and unexamined sampling choices can invalidate conclusions.
For each checklist item, record the evidence, the remaining uncertainty, and the next verification step.
